title: Edge-to-Cloud inference: gap analysis and sell threads
body:
Purpose:
This note is a tactical go-to-market brief for sales and solutions teams to use when prospects are evaluating building their own inference stack (vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM hybrids) versus buying Redwood (hosted / dedicated / private). It focuses on concrete operational gaps, realistic cost and latency tradeoffs, and high-leverage sell threads for edge or mixed edge/cloud requirements.

Audience:
- AE / SE pre-sales conversations with infra/platform buyers
- Solutions engineers preparing PoCs comparing self-hosted against Redwood Dedicated/Private
- Product marketing for messaging and collateral templates

TL;DR (elevator):
Most teams under-estimate ops cost and subtle latency tail risks when they pick off-the-shelf OSS stacks for inference. vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM give good control and raw perf in narrow scenarios, but Redwood wins on predictable economics, SLO-level fallbacks, and multi-env consistency (edge + cloud) — especially where customer apps need SLAs, mixed deployment modes, or operator headcount is constrained.

Key competitive technical differences (practical frame):
- Runtime predictability: OSS stacks vary with sequence length mix, KV-cache management, and multi-tenant interference. vLLM and TGI are flexible but require tedious tuning of batching and memory eviction to avoid latency spikes. Redwood’s runtime ships pre-tuned kernels + routing policies to reduce these tail events.
- Deployment heterogeneity: Self-hosted stacks excel when you control a single homogeneous fleet. They struggle when workloads cross edge (small devices), private datacenter, and cloud regions — porting quantization and kernel choices is a big friction point. Redwood provides the same API and rollout semantics across hosted/dedicated/private.
- Cost-per-token predictability: OSS can be cheaper on paper for very large, stable workloads that perfectly fit hardware. In practice, engineers rarely achieve ideal packing, leading to wasted GPU memory and suboptimal throughput. Redwood Optimize recommendations + autoscaling + prefix caching narrow that delta.
- Development velocity and evals: Building model validation, regression detection, and prompt-set-driven quality monitoring is non-trivial. vLLM/TGI users often lack integrated eval tooling. Redwood ties quality alerts to prompt sets and rollout policies.
- Safety & compliance: On-prem or VPC deployments with KMS/HSM integrations are possible OSS-side but require custom engineering and audit hooks; Redwood Private packages those integrations and retention policies out of the box.

Concrete failure modes we see in self-hosted trials (real examples to cite to prospects):
1) Latency tail after a rollout: new quantized model variant intermittently regresses for long-context chat requests because KV cache eviction policy wasn't adjusted. Customer sees 95th/99th spike — users complain.
2) Cold-start cost curve: bursty production traffic requires maintaining idle GPUs to meet SLOs, operator turns off GPUs to save cost and misses peak inflight traffic — customer loses conversions.
3) Hidden engineering debt: integrating telemetry for per-route token-cost, per-prompt evals, and automated canary rollback proves delayed by months.

Sample cost comparison (illustrative, simplified):
- Small startup bursty chat app (10 qps, 1k tokens per conversation):
  - DIY vLLM on spot GPUs: low baseline cost, high ops time; 20–40% probability of SLO violation during bursts.
  - Redwood Hosted/Dedicated: slightly higher $/token but predictable capacity and SLA-backed fallbacks.
- Mid-market SaaS (200 qps, mixed embeddings + chat):
  - DIY needs multi-type fleet (GPU for generation, CPU/accelerators for embeddings), custom autoscaler, and 2.0 FTEs ops.
  - Redwood Dedicated: single contract with autoscaling policies, model catalog, and integrated observability. Faster time-to-market for new features.
- Regulated enterprise with air-gapped requirements:
  - DIY often chosen but delays integration with audit/KMS and increases security review cycles.
  - Redwood Private reduces legal review time and operational unknowns.

Operational burden checklist (what prospects rarely budget for):
- Continuous model benchmarking for different input distributions
- Per-route cost breakdown and token accounting to finance
- Canary pipelines + automated rollbacks tied to prompt-based evals
- Tail latency debugging tooling (per-token profiling + kernel traces)
- Multi-quantization model library and compatibility matrix for GPU generations

Sales-facing positioning hooks (short):
- If you need predictable SLAs and measurable unit economics, Redwood shifts risk off your engineers.
- If you expect mixed deployment modes (edge + cloud + private), Redwood provides a single control plane and deployment abstraction.
- If you already have 2+ infra engineers owning inference, we recommend a hybrid path: Redwood Dedicated + short-term self-hosted experiments for specialized kernels.

Objection handling (common buyer claims and concise rebuttals):
- "OSS is free; we’ll save money." -> Free software + ops time != lower total cost. Provide our 12-month TCO example and show typical operator FTE assumptions. Offer a 3-month Dedicated pilot pricing to validate real-world $/token.
- "We need custom kernels/quant for edge." -> Redwood supports custom model variants and private deployments; we can accommodate specialized kernels in Redwood Private engagements.
- "We already have a PoC that looks fast." -> Ask about 95th/99th latency, rollout history, and cost per routed token as traffic scales. Offer a side-by-side benchmark with representative load.

Practical SE playbook for a 2-week evaluation
1) Discovery: collect target SLOs (p50/p95/p99), traffic profile (seq length distribution), and security constraints.
2) Quick perf baseline: run Redwood hosted sample with representative prompt set and record tail latency and cost metrics.
3) Simultaneous DIY check: ask prospect to run their vLLM/TGI config on a small fleet using a shared benchmark harness (provide our scripts). Capture op-ex gaps (time to triage, kernel tuning iterations).
4) Show regression detection: push a subtle prompt-set regression to both stacks and demonstrate automated rollback/fallback on Redwood.
5) Propose pilot: Dedicated with a one-month commit and a rollback clause; include a shared runbook and SOC2/compliance checklist if needed.

Collateral / artifacts to share with prospects (quick list):
- Lightweight benchmark harness (GH link) for side-by-side testing
- 12-month TCO workbook template (spreadsheet) with operator FTE assumptions and spot vs reserved GPU pricing rows
- Short case study: "How X moved from vLLM PoC to Redwood Dedicated in 6 weeks" (anecdotal)
- Checklist: "Edge-to-cloud readiness" (SLOs, quant compatibility, audit needs)

Recommended positioning copy (one-liners for decks/emails):
- "Keep your model freedom, offload the operational risk."
- "Same API. Multiple deployment modes. Predictable economics."

Example SE email template to kick off a trial:
Hi <Name>,

Appreciate the demo yesterday — based on our conversation I put together a short 2-week plan so we can validate the most important things quickly:
1) Baseline: run your representative prompt set against Redwood hosted and your vLLM/TGI stack.
2) Tail test: capture p95/p99 under burst patterns and a long-context drift scenario.
3) Ops delta: timebox one root-cause triage and catalog the engineering hours.

I’ll share the benchmark harness and a small cost workbook. If the results look good we can stand up a Dedicated pilot with a rollback clause.

Next steps / ask from SEs / AEs:
- Use this brief as a checklist when prepping for infra-heavy prospects.
- Attach the benchmark harness link in any self-hosted claim slides.
- If a prospect is fixated on cheapest $/token, push the TCO workbook; if they are worried about SLAs push the pilot commitment.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- Build a short public-facing one-pager that juxtaposes three realistic customer archetypes and their likely winners (DIY vs Redwood Hosted vs Redwood Dedicated).
- Add two short benchmark scripts to GH to automate p95/p99 sniffing under mixed-length sequences.
- Compile 3 anonymized customer anecdotes to use in Sales decks.

Notes to self (working):
- Coordinate with Product to see if we can add a sample kernel-compatibility matrix for common GPU families in the public docs.
- Track feedback from two pilot customers this quarter to quantify average ops FTE saved.

End of brief.
